summary: Nine systematic managers debate year-end 2024: risk vs uncertainty (trend and positive convexity as the answer), crypto/meme bubble, CTA replication, multi-strat growth and why alternatives are under-adopted. They discuss the dollar (cyclical positive, structurally overvalued) and trend positioning (long US equities, short bonds), with outrageous 2025 predictions.

coverage.note: intro/sponsor, agenda; Richard raises social media for awareness (no market content)
social media use by Andrew and Jim for awareness (no market content)
risk vs uncertainty: trend as robust, broad distributions
uncertainty and convexity, risk beyond vol; MicroStrategy and crypto bubble
bubble and animal spirits, intrinsic value, GFC risk tolerance
generational disaffection and inequality; replication debate begins
replication views of Rich, Katy; parameter diversification, tail protection access
replication views of Niels, Nick; Andrew starts on industry future
managed futures as attractive asset class, underallocated; product proliferation
end of falling rates, true alternatives, structured product flows, multi-strats rise
why multi-strats are liked, convergence vs divergence, scale model
multi-strat as free leverage on derivatives, cross-asset premia, CTA AUM stagnation
why adoption is low: Bridgewater in index, lack of economic conviction, alpha mindset
narrative for adoption, when vs why, US dislocation topic
dollar and BRICS, trend positioning, dollar drivers, correlations
cyclical vs secular dollar, Plaza accord, steeper curve
outrageous predictions 2025: China compromise, entitlements, Bitcoin, optimism
AI recession prediction; outro and plugs

claims.speaker: Katy Kaminski
claims.quote: trend is not about knowing what's going to happen it's about moving with what's happening
claims.claim: Much of life is uncertainty (unknowable), not countable risk, so simple trend rules that move with what is happening are robust.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: I think the distributions are easier to predict Than People expect or understand
claims.claim: Rather than predicting events, think in broad distributions across every vector and shift them for known structural pressures; this is a real edge.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: the only way I I see you can deal with it effectively is through positive complexity
claims.claim: In the chaotic tail regions uncertainty cannot be quantified, so positive convexity is the way to handle it; models that ignore uncertainty come undone when it hits.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: I also think of the uncertainty as the additional higher order effect of what is not anymore measurable even in the statistical error of estimating the inputs
claims.claim: Risk is volatility, correlation and estimation error; uncertainty is the higher-order remainder, so portfolio construction should allow for the unseen.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: the companies listed at a massive premium to it's nav which is mostly consists of Bitcoin
claims.claim: MicroStrategy at a big premium to NAV, levered Bitcoin ETFs, meme stocks and billion-dollar coins with 1% float look like a late-stage speculative bubble.
claims.indicator: MicroStrategy premium to NAV, meme/crypto issuance

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: I believe in intrinsic value and that doesn't seem to matter very much anymore
claims.claim: Intrinsic value matters less in the current speculative environment, with value investors disoriented by meme and crypto valuation.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: there is to me a sense a broad-based sense of of a Resurgence of animal spirits
claims.claim: After the election, a pro-business administration with self-made entrepreneurs revives animal spirits and risk-taking, after years of conservatism since the GFC.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: it is a function of Federal Reserve monetary policy driving inequality
claims.claim: Generational disaffection from inequality (a Fed policy effect) drives disruption and populist change as in the 1960s-70s, and persists for a generation.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: as time has passed you know performance seems to have been reasonably good
claims.claim: Replication was expected to be too slow and not trade enough markets, but its performance has been reasonably good and it is now an established way to run a managed futures program.
claims.testable: yes - compare replicator and CTA returns

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: if you are going to replicate then in my opinion bottom up is is a better way of doing it
claims.claim: Of top-down and bottom-up replication, bottom-up is better; cheap CTA exposure for ordinary people is what matters.

claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
claims.quote: there is replication risk in there um which and and I don't think we've got a sufficient enough track record to come out with a verdict yet
claims.claim: Replication lacks a long enough track record across regimes to judge its risk.

claims.speaker: Katy Kaminski
claims.quote: it tends to be a little slower but it does sort of give you generalized Dynamic exposure to overall themes and Trends in ctas
claims.claim: Replication is slower but gives generalized dynamic exposure to CTA themes, one of many access points.

claims.speaker: Katy Kaminski
claims.quote: fan of sort of the classic Trend falling technique about sort of diversifying across different parameter sets
claims.claim: Classic trend following diversifies across parameter sets, markets and strategies to capture crisis alpha.

claims.speaker: Katy Kaminski
claims.quote: so many investors have very little tear tail protection they don't have access to things that can be uncorrelated and diversified
claims.claim: Many investors lack tail protection and uncorrelated diversifiers, a case for wider access to CTA exposure.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: and it doesn't matter that you don't measure the underlying uh price data um maybe you can just get it through the performance data of of managers
claims.claim: A replicator can infer trend exposure from manager performance data rather than from price data.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: the nature of the replication is to succeed as well as the underlying does
claims.claim: A replicator can only match the underlying CTAs, so if managers change profile (e.g. reverse) the replicator follows them, an existential rather than technical risk.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: when stock and bond correlations are POS are positive you get every dollar you generate as a result of that shows up as Alpha
claims.claim: Managed futures is uncorrelated to stocks and bonds; this matters now that stock-bond correlation is positive, it does best when needed and has no gates or lock-ups.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: maybe 8% in of their portfolio in hedge funds of which maybe 5% of that is managed Futures
claims.claim: Managed futures is underinvested: institutions hold about 8% in hedge funds, about 5% of which is managed futures (about 50 bp of the portfolio).

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: as you have pressure on interest rates to at least mean revert if not go higher over this coming period
claims.claim: After 40 years of falling rates, higher rates cut expected returns on bonds and stocks, so true alternatives (non-correlated derivatives) are needed.
claims.direction: stocks and bonds lower return, alternatives up

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: private Equity ventured Capital uh real estate are not Alternatives despite what they've been marketed
claims.claim: Private equity, VC and real estate are not true alternatives because they are equity/duration beta; true alternatives are non-correlated derivative strategies.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: double doubling in size of Structured Products annual issuance and a 7x increase in ETFs tied to options
claims.claim: Flows into structured products and option/managed-futures ETFs are growing fast, the early stage of adopting non-correlated investments as 60/40 loses appeal.
claims.indicator: structured product issuance, option ETF assets

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: the other big Trend we've seen in the markets over five years which dominates everything is the rise of the multi strats
claims.claim: Multi-strats grew from a fraction of 2019 assets to dominate the hedge fund industry in five years, and return stacking, QIS and replication moved from skepticism to mainstream.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: why do people like the multiat so much it's you know consistency of performance not necessarily convey not necessarily very strong returns
claims.claim: Institutions favour multi-strats for steady ~8% returns, which conflicts with the demand for diversifying alternatives.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: I'd be optimistic on Trend following manage Futures becoming more embedded in portfolios over a 5-year view
claims.claim: Investor perception of managed futures improved after 2021-22 from the weak 2010s, so allocations should rise over five years.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: this is the ultimate convergent versus Divergence set of strategies multi strats in general do not do Trend following
claims.claim: Multi-strats are convergence strategies (low vol, high alpha, levered) while trend followers are divergence strategies, so they are competing worldviews on how to make money.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: what an Amazon can do as both an operator and a capital allocator in a sense the multi strats are doing
claims.claim: Multi-strats succeed through scale as operator and capital allocator (teams, infrastructure, best terms), a different model from funds of funds, so the 180th pod need not be worse.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: that ability to leverage for free is what is generating these returns and the higher interest rates go the more you can make on that leverage
claims.claim: Multi-strat returns come from the capital efficiency of derivatives (free leverage on diversified edge) and rise with interest rates, so higher rates benefit them.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: when stock flation came along and the macro Dynamics are such where by there is no return to be harvested in conventional markets
claims.claim: Cross-asset risk premia and multi-strat strategies returned because investors needed diversifying returns when stagflation left conventional markets without return.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: it is still kind of fluctuating around the 350 Mark that has been around for the last maybe
claims.claim: Barclay CTA index AUM has stayed near $350bn for about 14 years, so adoption of managed futures has been flat despite the evidence.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: there is one firm in that number that makes up a very large part of it and I don't consider them as a CTA and that's Bridgewater
claims.claim: The CTA AUM index is distorted by Bridgewater, which is not a CTA; some CTA-like assets sit outside databases.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: this lack of economic conviction that it should work in the first place
claims.claim: Investors see statistical benefit and backtests but lack an economic reason it should work, which limits adoption.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: when you describe managed Futures to them there's just this kind of collective sense of disappointment
claims.claim: Allocators trained to look for information-based alpha and mispricing are disappointed by managed futures because it earns by following movements, not by explaining value.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: figure out a narrative around it that makes people like it and want it
claims.claim: A narrative for why trend following belongs in a portfolio would bring adoption, since the statistical case already exists.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: if you ask someone would you rather know the why or the when a market is going to move I would have thought the when is more interesting more profitable than knowing why
claims.claim: Knowing when a market will move is more profitable than knowing why, which favours timing/trend over explanatory narratives.

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: we are seeing a historic dislocation between the United States and performance relative to the rest of the world
claims.claim: US outperformance versus the rest of the world is historically large; knowing when it normalises (driven by dollar and Fed policy) could pay well.
claims.indicator: US vs rest of world relative performance

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I wonder a little bit whether it's going to have any effect whatsoever
claims.claim: Talk of BRICS de-dollarisation is widely discussed but may have no effect on the dollar's reserve role for now.

claims.speaker: Katy Kaminski
claims.quote: Trend signals have moved very long equities particularly us um short fixed income but also long the dollar in size
claims.claim: Trend signals in Dec 2024 were long US equities, short fixed income and long the dollar after a V-shaped dollar move; the question is how long it lasts.
claims.direction: long US equities, short bonds, long USD

claims.speaker: Katy Kaminski
claims.quote: the US dollar is always tricky because it's a combination of sentiment It's a combination of monetary policy
claims.claim: The dollar combines sentiment, monetary policy and US growth; the pro-growth outlook and cautious Fed support the trend short-term but the long-run is unclear.

claims.speaker: Katy Kaminski
claims.quote: how much um a change in policy and deficits and things have the ability to create more disruptive correlations
claims.claim: Inflation uncertainty, policy and deficits can make cross-asset correlations more disruptive, so a wider range of macro outcomes is likely.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: in contrast to Europe which is totally in the Dos um rates are definitely going to be cut Europe so that's the kind of the cyclical Dynamic is looking dollar positive
claims.claim: Cyclically the dollar is positive: US animal spirits may force the Fed to raise rates again while Europe cuts.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: they want to have a lower dollar to balance trade but at the same time you don't want to if you have a weakening of the dollar then who's going to fund the deficit
claims.claim: Structurally the dollar is overvalued, but a weaker dollar raises the problem of funding the deficit and reserve status, so a managed decline is hard.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
claims.quote: we may see a plaza type of cord at some point particularly if the dollar appreciates again
claims.claim: A Plaza-type accord (as in 1985) could be used for a coordinated dollar decline if the dollar overshoots further.

claims.speaker: Katy Kaminski
claims.quote: also potential for steeper in the guild curve at some point
claims.claim: The yield curve may steepen (a 2024 prediction that held).

claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
claims.quote: Trump much like Nixon reaches across and makes some grand um compromise with China which means the reversion of Chinese assets relative to the rest of the world
claims.claim: After tariff bluster, a Trump-China compromise like Nixon's would revive Chinese assets relative to the rest of the world, a big 2025 trade.
claims.indicator: Chinese assets vs rest of world

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: could result in a very different interest rate outcome than I think people are probably expecting from a trump Administration
claims.claim: If the administration tackles entitlements and the structural deficit, rates could differ from expectations (lower term premium).

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: Bitcoin 200,000 and I hope I'm wrong
claims.claim: Bitcoin to 200,000 in 2025 as a joke-prediction of the bubble continuing.

claims.speaker: Mark Rzepczynski
claims.quote: we naturally have a bias always to be negative we always want to be doomsdayers
claims.claim: Forecasters have a negativity bias, so crisis calls are over-predicted and an optimistic baseline is reasonable.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: us 10-year treasury yield crashes to 1% in recession of AI prediction
claims.claim: A sudden AI-driven layoff recession with deflation fears and a safe-haven rush would send the 10-year yield to 1%; the speaker does not really believe it.
